props.covers: The operational-map diagram language: the two genres every board mixes, the object surface — eight universal shapes plus the 30-glyph roster — and the preference registry that keeps boards consistent, closed by the decisions that shaped the language.

text.insert: What an operational map is, the two genres every board mixes, the object surface of eight universal shapes plus a 95-glyph icon vocabulary, and the preference registry that keeps boards consistent. The decisions that shaped the language close the doc.

Two genres, applied per region, not per board. Any region of a board is either mapping structure or walking a procedure, and the region's genre fixes its vocabulary, what its edges mean, and its reading direction. This section is the build grammar: the description the system uses to decide what it is drawing, and the reason two boards of the same system come out looking alike.
, with about two-thirds of all edges temporal (next step, branch, ordering) and one-third data relationships (reads, writes, feeds, informs). The split is the genre boundary made visible.

, and a system map's section can itself be a procedure (the map shows the factory, one section walks a single machine's loop). Procedures sit inside mapped components and maps form context around a central procedure, but neither frames the other by rule.

(an edge from a procedure step writing into a memory node is a procedure node touching a map node). Control flow that periodically touches shared state is the signature of an agentic-system board, the most agentic content on it.

for drawing a region is to decide its genre first, and the genre then fixes the vocabulary (components and stores versus steps and branches), what the edges mean, and the reading direction. Applying the same decision procedure every time is what makes boards consistent.

Icons carry the semantic vocabulary, and shapes are a small universal core. Icons win because they have better detail, come from vendored icon sets through generators (expanding the set is selection, not authoring), need no bespoke geometry maintenance, and are user-swappable: customizing your diagram style means picking a different glyph. A shape earns its place only by being universally readable without a legend while holding a name inside a resizable outline. Section, sticky, and connector are permanent fixtures outside the shape roster, and the pill look belongs solely to the connector's label chip and is not a placeable object.

The full placeable shape roster is eight universal marks. Arrow and triangle keep the schema's direction field (arrow: left or right, triangle: up or down), placed as directional variants the way the picker already offers them:
is a plain box for a message or payload container
is a delegated step: spawned sub-agent, subroutine, enqueued task
is a directional marker with direction up or down
serves as start and end terminators, kept for universality more than corpus usage
is a routing outcome with direction left or right
Everything else in the basic and flowchart categories is cut.

The document / file / page-corner family collapses into one well-chosen document glyph; storage cylinders yield to the database glyph; the picker's default face is icons, with this shape core as a small utility row.

Every shape, icon, and section carries a short name and at most one detail line. The name says what the thing is in about five words on one line. The detail is one muted fact under it, such as a port, path, version, model, or host, in 48 characters or fewer. Prose goes on a Markdown sticky beside its subject: the why, the how, caveats, and examples. Two lint warnings enforce it:
flags a name over six words or 40 characters, or with a sentence or line break, and
flags a detail over 48 characters, with a second sentence, or with a line break.

The generic glyphs name roles and infrastructure the operational-map corpus lacks, and the brand logos name concrete products. Every glyph picker (the Shapes panel and the Inspector's Glyph and Icon fields) groups glyphs by category, brands last, and searches labels, ids, and category names:
Any glyph can also be a section's header icon, drawn before the title in the header chip. Give a section an icon when a glyph fits what the region holds: a generic glyph for its role, such as

, or a brand logo for a technology the board names. When no glyph fits, the section has no icon, and an icon never decorates. A person sets it in the Inspector's Icon field, and the layout agent sets it with

Every semantic object gets a registry entry: its name, what it means, the scenarios where it is used, and its default color. The name is the stored glyph or shape id itself, one string across registry, picker, agent vocabulary, and lints, with no separate render pointer. Defaults carry consistency: the default color and the shared meaning cover the vast majority of placements. Color is the one per-placement override, for legibility against a section's fill or a board's palette, while meaning and scenarios are shared language and do not vary. Their main consumer is the agent's context, the vocabulary listing of every shape and glyph, plus picker tooltips and lint wording.

beside it: 103 entries, the 8 shapes first, then the 95 glyphs in roster order. The order is load-bearing. The agent's vocabulary listing walks it as-is, and the picker keeps it within each category group.

The context renderer. registry.context renders the vocabulary the agent reads: one element per object, walked in roster order (shapes first, then glyphs). Each element carries the name, the default color, the meaning, and one line per scenario. XML keeps each object a visually distinct block in the prompt. The format is otherwise unimportant. This listing replaces the hand-maintained capabilities vocabulary. The registry becomes its single source.

<vocabulary>
  <object name="decision" preferred_color="gray">
    <meaning>A branch — the flow forks on a condition</meaning>
    <use_when>
      - yes/no gates
      - routing on the outcome of a check
    </use_when>
  </object>
  <object name="memory" preferred_color="blue">
    <meaning>A store an agent reads from or writes to across turns</meaning>
    <use_when>
      - long/short-term memory, knowledge bases, vector stores
      - the target of state-read / state-write edges
    </use_when>
  </object>
  <object name="agent" preferred_color="teal">
    <meaning>An autonomous agent — plans and acts on its own</meaning>
    <use_when>
      - main agents, sub-agents, workers in a pool
    </use_when>
  </object>
  <!-- … one element per shape and glyph, roster order … -->
</vocabulary>

Storage and editing. The registry is not a service. It is a JSON file in the repo, the shipped base corpus, and the single source every consumer reads. Two things read it: the context renderer above and the picker (labels, tooltips, creation colors). The lints quote it for wording. One thing writes it: a registry editor in the studio config surface, where meanings, use-when lists, and preferred colors are adjusted per entry. Edits change the shared defaults themselves (the whole system's language moves together), and a change regenerates the picker's catalog and the agent's context listing. Per-placement color changes are not registry writes. They live on the board object, one at a time.

Placement and color. Creation does not accept a color, and that is a feature, not a gap: placing an object stamps the registry's preferred color, and recoloring is its own later gesture (change_color). The two-step forces the right thinking: place it, then look at the board and ask whether this spot warrants a different color at all. The agent's loop already supports this literally: every placement attaches a fresh draft render to the pushed state, so the agent sees the default-colored object in situ before any recolor decision. Most of the time the answer is the default, which is the consistency working.
The canvas is Core's map layer, designed for agentic systems; other diagram forms are incidental. When design choices pull apart, the agentic use case wins.

props.title: Free composition. Depth lives in the docs

text.insert: No enforced containment or layout templates: sections are available structure, not mandatory. Boards stay operational. Detailed diagrams (sequence, fine-grained flow) live in doc sections beside an embedded reference view of the board region.

props.title: Icon-first with an eight-shape universal core

text.insert: Icons carry semantics; the placeable shapes are exactly the eight listed above, with arrow (left/right) and triangle (up/down) as directional variants. Predefined process stays a shape (needs inline text, reads universally). Pill is connector furniture only. The document family collapses into a single glyph.

props.title: One canonical name per object, everywhere

text.insert: The registry's key field is name, and that string is the single canonical id across the whole system: registry key, picker label, the string the agent types to place the object, and the string lints cite. There is no renders field: the name IS the stored glyph or shape id, so an entry cannot drift from the art it names. Changing the art behind a name is a manifest change and a regeneration, not a registry alias.

The registry ships a default base corpus (meanings, scenarios, colors), and the defaults cover the vast majority of placements. Most boards use them unmodified. Color is the single per-placement override, warranted by section fills and palette collisions. Meaning and scenarios are shared language, fixed across users and boards, and their primary consumer is the agent's context: the vocabulary listing that teaches the system what each object is and when to use it. Overrides ripple to the picker and the agent via the registry.changed event.

props.title: Edge style stays soft, with round caps and joins in both packs

text.insert: The nucleo_sharp set (24px, square caps, miter corners) was evaluated via rendered contact sheets and rejected: the softer nucleo_ui/outline style reads better. The 30 operational-map glyphs draw from nucleo_ui/outline at 18px in the nucleo pack, and the generic glyphs come from Tabler's outline set, which shares the round caps and joins. Both render at one stroke weight across their grids.

props.title: A brand logo names the exact product

text.insert: A brand logo asserts a specific technology, so it appears only where the diagram names that product, and the generic glyph carries the role everywhere else: PostgreSQL gets
. The logos come from a pinned Simple Icons release with each logo's license recorded, and the roster carries no AWS or OpenAI logos.

props.title: The connection role field is deleted

text.insert: Connections carry exactly what a reader can see: the on-line text (label), arrowhead, line style, and color. The invisible role string (schema-allowed, never rendered, never settable in the UI, written only by the layout agent and read back only by its own digest) is removed from the schema, the agent surface, and the digest, with existing boards stripped by migration. Edge meaning lives on the line: the label carries it for a reader, and conventional looks for recurring edge kinds are general prompting guidance. This closes the edge-encoding question.

props.title: Color overrides: one guidance sentence, one lint

text.insert: Two mechanisms, both small. The agent context carries one sentence of guidance: keep preferred colors, and depart only when the object would sit illegibly in its container. And a new report-only lint warns when a direct child of a container shares the container's color: a red section must not hold red objects. Nothing blocks, nothing nags the human side. The registry default plus these two keep color drift in check.

props.title: Visual Patterns as Shared Design Guidance

text.insert: A shared visual pattern library explains how fan-out, convergence, hierarchy, sequence, feedback, transformation, comparison, separation, and shared resources express behavior. Patterns are composable reference material, not fixed layout templates. The agent chooses them from the subject and preserves consistent treatment for equivalent roles. Multi-zoom composition, shape meaning, and color meaning accompany the library in standing context. Depth assessment is an explicit system-prompt phase after orientation. Core philosophy lives in the system prompt directly after purpose. The quality checklist lives in the system prompt's success criteria, after the workflow and before the final rules. The system prompt now follows the behavioral reference's sequence: orientate, assess depth and evidence, understand the subject, map patterns, build incrementally, verify the rendered explanation with visual checks and lint evidence, then finalize. Measured lint checks support defect review, while conceptual quality remains a judgment against the rendered diagram and its source.

documents stays a stack because a pile of files is how that thing actually looks. Nothing else gets plural art. Many agents are drawn as structure (a fan-out from the delegating step to its workers), not as a dedicated icon, and counts live in text when they matter. No custom stacked art is composed.

props.title: The genre is named the operational map

text.insert: Boards of this kind are operational maps, in the docs, in the agent prompting, and in UI copy. Short form: op map. Runners-up (living blueprint, system board, leveled system map) are retired.
Sections have no ports. Cross-section edges attach to the section itself and mean all-of-this. Revisit only if free composition proves to need boundary termination.
